RagShortTexts: Stirling Castle commanded the narrow Forth crossing, revered as the indispensable military.

Variants.Content: Stirling Castle commanded the lowest crossing of the River Forth, the point where an army moving north from the Lowlands had to cross or go around a wide flood plain. The castle rose on a volcanic crag, and whoever held it controlled the road into the Highlands. Stirling Bridge, fought in 1297, showed how the boggy carse and a narrow bridge could trap a larger force, and the castle changed hands repeatedly through the Wars of Scottish Independence. Its garrison and royal officers could block a royal army, tax river traffic, and set the terms of any northern campaign, which made the fortress a prize that every Scottish and English king wanted to hold.

A Scottish lord who holds land west of the castle owes his service to the garrison, and the captain keeps a careful eye on which clans answer the summons. Soldiers marching out learn the carse early: wet ground sucks at the boots, and the bridge is narrow enough for one horse at a time. Keep your shield up on the approach and never leave the causeway to chase a flanking rider.
